about: The scripted AI lesson for p3-density (2026-11-17, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p3-particle-model.

keyPoints.heading: What density is and why it matters

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about why some things float and others sink, and how one number can tell you what a material is.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from the last lesson. In which state are the particles far apart, with empty space between them?
steps.right: Yes: in a gas the particles are far apart.

wrong.other: Not quite: a gas.
wrong.solid: Not quite: solid particles are packed close together in a regular pattern. Far apart is a gas.
wrong.liquid: Not quite: liquid particles touch each other. Far apart is a gas.

idk.hint: In a solid and in a liquid, the particles touch each other. Which state is left?

steps.answerWhy: In a gas the particles are far apart, with empty space between them.

steps.question: Second: 200 g of ice melts. What is the mass of the water?
steps.right: Yes: 200 g. Mass stays the same in a change of state.

wrong.other: Not quite: 200 g. Mass stays the same in a change of state.
wrong.less: Not quite: no particles are lost when ice melts, so the water is still 200 g.
wrong.more: Not quite: no particles are added when ice melts, so the water is still 200 g.

idk.hint: No particles are made or destroyed when ice melts. So which mass must the water have?

steps.answerWhy: Mass stays the same in a change of state, so the water is 200 g.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Mass is how much matter something has. It is measured in kilograms (kg) or grams (g): 1 kg = 1000 g.
Volume is how much space something takes up. It is measured in cubic metres (m³) or cubic centimetres (cm³): a cube 1 cm along each side has a volume of 1 cm³.
A bag of flour and a bag of popcorn can be the same size, yet the flour is far heavier. The flour packs more mass into the same volume.
The mass in each cubic metre, or in each cubic centimetre, of a material is called the density of the material.
The symbol for density is ρ, the Greek letter rho. The equation is ρ = m ÷ V: density = mass ÷ volume.
In the equation, ρ is the density in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³), m is the mass in kilograms (kg), and V is the volume in cubic metres (m³).
Grams and cubic centimetres also work together: then the density comes out in g/cm³. Water has a density of 1000 kg/m³, which is 1 g/cm³.

steps.question: Block A has a mass of 10 g and a volume of 10 cm³. Block B has a mass of 10 g and a volume of 5 cm³. Which is denser?
steps.right: Yes: B packs the same mass into half the space. Its density is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 g/cm³; A's is 10 ÷ 10 = 1 g/cm³.

wrong.other: Not quite: block B.
wrong.bigger: Not quite: A is bigger, so its mass is more spread out. B packs the same mass into half the space, so B is denser.
wrong.same: Not quite: density is mass for each cm³, not mass alone. B fits its 10 g into half the volume, so B is denser.

idk.hint: Density is mass ÷ volume. Work out 10 ÷ 10 and 10 ÷ 5.

steps.answerWhy: A: 10 ÷ 10 = 1 g/cm³. B: 10 ÷ 5 = 2 g/cm³. B is denser.

steps.text: A material is dense when its particles are heavy, or packed tightly, or both.
Whether something floats depends on density, not on how heavy it is. An object floats in a liquid or gas that is denser than the object, and sinks in one that is less dense.
A huge log floats on water because wood is less dense than water, while a small nail sinks because iron is denser: about 7900 kg/m³.

steps.question: Ice has a density of 920 kg/m³. Water's is 1000 kg/m³. Will an ice cube float or sink in water?

options.text: It floats only if it is small

steps.right: Yes: 920 kg/m³ is less than water's 1000 kg/m³, so ice floats.

wrong.other: Not quite: it floats, because 920 kg/m³ is less than 1000 kg/m³.
wrong.sinks: Not quite: most solids are denser than their liquid, but water is an exception. 920 kg/m³ is less than 1000 kg/m³, so ice floats.
wrong.small: Not quite: size does not decide it; density does. 920 kg/m³ is less than 1000 kg/m³, so any ice cube floats.

idk.hint: An object less dense than water floats. Is 920 less than 1000?

steps.answerWhy: 920 kg/m³ is less than water's 1000 kg/m³, so ice floats.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does density mean?
points: the mass in each unit of volume (mass ÷ volume)
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: density is how much mass there is in each cubic metre (or cm³): mass ÷ volume.

steps.text: Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A block of pine has a mass of 600 g and a volume of 1000 cm³. What is its density?
steps: Write the equation: ρ = m ÷ V.

steps.question: Your turn. A stone has a mass of 300 g and a volume of 120 cm³. What is its density, in g/cm³?

wrong.other: Not quite: 2.5 g/cm³. ρ = m ÷ V = 300 ÷ 120 = 2.5 g/cm³.
wrong.times: Not quite: 2.5 g/cm³. Divide the mass by the volume, do not multiply: 300 ÷ 120 = 2.5.
wrong.upside: Not quite: 2.5 g/cm³. Mass goes on top: 300 ÷ 120, not 120 ÷ 300.

idk.hint: Use ρ = m ÷ V: divide the mass, 300, by the volume, 120.

steps.question: Some densities: aluminium 2.7 g/cm³, iron 7.9 g/cm³, gold 19.3 g/cm³. A shiny block has a mass of 79 g and a volume of 10 cm³. Which metal is it?
steps.right: Yes: 79 ÷ 10 = 7.9 g/cm³, which matches iron. Density tells you what a material is.

wrong.other: Not quite: iron. 79 ÷ 10 = 7.9 g/cm³.
wrong.gold: Not quite: gold would be 19.3 g/cm³. This block is 79 ÷ 10 = 7.9 g/cm³: iron.
wrong.alu: Not quite: aluminium would be 2.7 g/cm³. This block is 79 ÷ 10 = 7.9 g/cm³: iron.

idk.hint: Work out its density first: 79 ÷ 10. Then find that number in the list.

steps.answerWhy: The block's density is 79 ÷ 10 = 7.9 g/cm³, which matches iron.

steps.text: To find a mass or a volume, put the numbers into ρ = m ÷ V first, then rearrange. Rearranged, m = ρ × V and V = m ÷ ρ. Use a calculator for the sums.
Here is a worked example of finding a mass. Its steps open one at a time.
steps.question: A gold ring has a volume of 0.8 cm³. Gold has a density of 19.3 g/cm³. What is the ring's mass?
steps: Put the numbers into ρ = m ÷ V: 19.3 = m ÷ 0.8.

steps.question: A tank holds 2 m³ of oil. The oil has a density of 900 kg/m³. What is the oil's mass, in kg?

wrong.divide: Not quite: you divided 900 by 2. Mass = density × volume: 900 × 2 = 1800 kg.
wrong.upside: Not quite: you divided 2 by 900. Mass = density × volume: 900 × 2 = 1800 kg.

idk.hint: Put the numbers in: 900 = m ÷ 2. Then multiply both sides by 2.

steps.text: Here is a worked example of finding a volume. Its steps open one at a time.
steps.question: A 600 g piece of wood has a density of 0.5 g/cm³. What is its volume?
steps: Put the numbers into ρ = m ÷ V: 0.5 = 600 ÷ V.
Multiply both sides by V: 0.5 × V = 600.
Divide both sides by 0.5: V = 600 ÷ 0.5 = 1200 cm³.

steps.question: A 2000 kg block of concrete has a density of 2500 kg/m³. What is its volume, in m³?

wrong.times: Not quite: you multiplied. Volume = mass ÷ density: 2000 ÷ 2500 = 0.8 m³.
wrong.upside: Not quite: you divided the density by the mass. Volume = mass ÷ density: 2000 ÷ 2500 = 0.8 m³.

idk.hint: Put the numbers in: 2500 = 2000 ÷ V. Multiply both sides by V, then divide both sides by 2500.

steps.text: Watch the units. 1 kg is 1000 g, and 1 m³ is 1 000 000 cm³, so 1 g/cm³ is the same as 1000 kg/m³. Multiply by 1000 to go from g/cm³ to kg/m³; divide by 1000 to go back.

steps.question: Iron has a density of 7900 kg/m³. What is that in g/cm³?

wrong.other: Not quite: 7.9 g/cm³. Divide by 1000.
wrong.times: Not quite: going from kg/m³ to g/cm³, divide by 1000: 7900 ÷ 1000 = 7.9 g/cm³.
wrong.same: Not quite: the number changes with the units. Divide by 1000: 7.9 g/cm³.

steps.text: A substance's density changes when it melts, because its volume changes. Most solids take up a little more space as a liquid, so the liquid is a little less dense.

steps.question: A 2.7 kg block of solid has a volume of 0.001 m³. It melts, and the liquid has a volume of 0.00108 m³. What is the liquid's density, in kg/m³?
steps.right: Yes: 2500 kg/m³. The mass is still 2.7 kg, so ρ = 2.7 ÷ 0.00108 = 2500 kg/m³.

wrong.other: Not quite: 2500 kg/m³. The mass is still 2.7 kg, so ρ = 2.7 ÷ 0.00108 = 2500 kg/m³.
wrong.solid: Not quite: 2700 kg/m³ is the solid. Use the liquid's volume: 2.7 ÷ 0.00108 = 2500 kg/m³.
wrong.times: Not quite: divide the mass by the volume: 2.7 ÷ 0.00108 = 2500 kg/m³.

idk.hint: The mass is still 2.7 kg. On a calculator, divide it by the liquid's volume, 0.00108.

steps.answerWhy: The mass stays 2.7 kg, so ρ = 2.7 ÷ 0.00108 = 2500 kg/m³.

steps.prompt: In one line: how do you find a volume from a density and a mass?
points: divide the mass by the density (V = m ÷ ρ), or put the numbers into ρ = m ÷ V and rearrange
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: put the numbers into ρ = m ÷ V, then rearrange to V = m ÷ ρ: mass divided by density.

keyPoints.heading: Measuring density in the lab (required practical)

steps.question: To find the density of a stone, which two things do you need to measure?
steps.right: Yes: then density = mass ÷ volume.

wrong.other: Not quite: its mass and its volume.
wrong.length: Not quite: a length alone is not a volume. You need its mass and its volume.
wrong.temp: Not quite: temperature is not in the equation. You need its mass and its volume.

idk.hint: Look at the equation ρ = m ÷ V. Which two quantities are on the right?

steps.answerWhy: ρ = m ÷ V, so you need the mass and the volume.

steps.text: Measuring density is a required practical: the exam can ask you to describe how to do it.
A balance is the lab's weighing scales: it measures mass, in grams. First check it reads zero with nothing on it. If it reads 0.02 g when empty, take 0.02 g off every reading.
For a regular solid, such as a cube or a cuboid, measure its length, width and height with a ruler. Its volume = length × width × height.
For a cylinder, measure its radius and height: V = π × r² × h. For a small object, a micrometer or Vernier callipers measure lengths more precisely than a ruler.

steps.question: A cuboid is 2 cm long, 3 cm wide and 5 cm high. Its mass is 81 g. What is its density, in g/cm³?
steps.right: Yes: 2.7 g/cm³. Volume = 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 cm³, so ρ = 81 ÷ 30 = 2.7 g/cm³.

wrong.other: Not quite: 2.7 g/cm³. Volume = 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 cm³, and ρ = 81 ÷ 30 = 2.7 g/cm³.
wrong.added: Not quite: 2.7 g/cm³. Multiply the sides for the volume, do not add them: 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 cm³. Then 81 ÷ 30 = 2.7.
wrong.upside: Not quite: 2.7 g/cm³. Mass goes on top: 81 ÷ 30 = 2.7 g/cm³.

idk.hint: First the volume: multiply 2 × 3 × 5. Then divide the mass, 81, by it.

steps.answerWhy: Volume = 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 cm³, so ρ = 81 ÷ 30 = 2.7 g/cm³.

steps.text: An irregular object, such as a stone, has no simple sides to measure. Instead, lower it into water and measure how much water it pushes aside: that is the displacement method.
A measuring cylinder is a tall glass or plastic tube with a volume scale up its side, in cm³.
To find a stone's volume with one, half fill the measuring cylinder with water and read the level. Lower the stone in on a thin thread, so it is fully under the water, and read the new level.

steps.question: The level reads 40 cm³ before the stone goes in and 52 cm³ after. What is the stone's volume, in cm³?
steps.right: Yes: 12 cm³. The rise in level is the stone's volume: 52 − 40 = 12 cm³.

wrong.other: Not quite: 12 cm³. The rise in level is the stone's volume: 52 − 40 = 12 cm³.
wrong.mean: Not quite: 12 cm³. Do not average the readings; subtract them: 52 − 40 = 12 cm³.
wrong.add: Not quite: 12 cm³. The stone only adds the rise in level: 52 − 40 = 12 cm³.

idk.hint: The stone pushed the water up. By how much did the level rise?

steps.answerWhy: The rise in level is the stone's volume: 52 − 40 = 12 cm³.

steps.text: Another way uses a eureka can: a can with a spout, filled with water up to the spout. Lower the object in, and the water it pushes out runs into a measuring cylinder. The volume of that water equals the volume of the object.
For a liquid: find the mass of an empty measuring cylinder, pour in some liquid and read its volume, then find the mass again. The liquid's mass is the second mass minus the first.

steps.question: Why should your eye be level with the water when you read a measuring cylinder?

options.text: So the reading is not too high or too low
So the water does not spill

steps.right: Yes: looking from above or below makes the level seem higher or lower than it is.

wrong.other: Not quite: so the reading is not too high or too low.
wrong.spill: Not quite: your eye cannot stop a spill. Looking from above or below makes the level seem higher or lower than it is.
wrong.sink: Not quite: where you look does not change the stone. Looking from above or below misreads the level.

idk.hint: Looking from above, the level seems to be in a different place. Which option is about getting the reading right?

steps.answerWhy: Looking from above or below makes the reading too high or too low, so read it with your eye level.

steps.text: Even with care, repeat readings scatter a little: too high one time, too low the next, for example from judging where the water level is. These are called random errors.

steps.question: Why is the mean (average) of three repeat readings better than one reading?

options.text: The highs and lows partly cancel out
In case the first one was measured wrong

steps.right: Yes: in a mean the highs and lows partly cancel, so it reduces the effect of random errors. An odd result also stands out, so you can leave it out.

wrong.other: Not quite: the highs and lows partly cancel out.
wrong.wrong: Close: a repeat can catch a slip. The main reason is that highs and lows partly cancel in a mean, which reduces the effect of random errors.
wrong.stop: Not quite: repeats cannot stop odd results, but they help you spot them. The highs and lows partly cancel in a mean.

idk.hint: Some readings are a bit too high and some a bit too low. What happens to them when you average?

steps.answerWhy: In a mean the highs and lows partly cancel, so it reduces the effect of random errors.

steps.prompt: In one line: how do you find the volume of a stone?
points: put it into water in a measuring cylinder (or a eureka can)
the rise in the level (or the water pushed out) is its volume
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: lower the stone into water in a measuring cylinder; the rise in the water level is its volume.

steps.text: Now back to particles. A gas is far less dense than a solid or a liquid: most of a gas is empty space, so each cubic metre holds very little mass.
Air has a density of only about 1.2 kg/m³, so water is more than 800 times denser than air.

In a solid and in a liquid the particles are close together, so their densities are similar. A solid's particles are packed tightly in a regular pattern, so it is usually a little denser than its liquid.

steps.question: A gas is squashed into a smaller volume. Which is true of its density?

options.text: It rises: the same mass in less volume
It stays the same: it is the same gas

steps.right: Yes: the mass stays the same but the volume shrinks, so ρ = m ÷ V gets bigger.

wrong.other: Not quite: it rises, because the same mass is in less volume.
wrong.falls: Not quite: the mass stays the same and the volume shrinks, so m ÷ V gets bigger: the density rises.
wrong.same: Not quite: same gas, but the particles are now closer together. Same mass in less volume means a higher density.

idk.hint: In ρ = m ÷ V, the mass stays the same. What happens to m ÷ V when V gets smaller?

steps.answerWhy: The mass stays the same and the volume shrinks, so the density rises.

steps.prompt: In one line: why are a solid and its liquid similar in density?
points: in both the particles are close together (touching)
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: in a solid and in its liquid the particles are close together, so the same space holds about the same mass.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: a 40 g block has a volume of 20 cm³. What is its density, in g/cm³?
steps.right: Yes: ρ = m ÷ V = 40 ÷ 20 = 2 g/cm³.

wrong.other: Not quite: 2 g/cm³. ρ = m ÷ V = 40 ÷ 20 = 2 g/cm³.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: a liquid has a density of 0.8 g/cm³. What is the mass of 50 cm³ of it, in g?
Quiz, question 3 of 6: which instrument measures the mass of a stone?
steps.right: Yes: a balance.

wrong.other: Not quite: a balance.
wrong.w1: Not quite: a ruler measures lengths. Mass is measured on a balance.
wrong.w2: Not quite: a measuring cylinder measures volume. Mass is measured on a balance.

steps.answerWhy: Mass is measured on a balance.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: the water in a measuring cylinder reads 30 cm³, and 38 cm³ with a bolt in it. What is the bolt's volume, in cm³?
steps.right: Yes: 38 − 30 = 8 cm³.

wrong.other: Not quite: 8 cm³. Subtract: 38 − 30 = 8 cm³.

steps.answerWhy: The rise in level is the bolt's volume: 38 − 30 = 8 cm³.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: an object has a density of 1200 kg/m³. Will it float or sink in water?
steps.right: Yes: 1200 kg/m³ is more than water's 1000 kg/m³, so it sinks.

wrong.other: Not quite: it sinks, because 1200 kg/m³ is more than 1000 kg/m³.
wrong.w2: Not quite: density decides it, not mass. 1200 kg/m³ is more than water's 1000 kg/m³, so it sinks.

steps.answerWhy: The object is denser than water (1000 kg/m³), so it sinks.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: which of these is the least dense?
steps.right: Yes: steam, a gas, with its particles far apart.

wrong.other: Not quite: steam.
wrong.w1: Not quite: in water the particles touch. Steam is a gas, with its particles far apart, so it is far less dense.
wrong.w2: Not quite: ice is a little less dense than water, but steam, a gas, is far less dense than both.

steps.answerWhy: Steam is a gas, so its particles are far apart and its density is far lower.

steps.text: That's the end of the quiz: you got {right} out of {n}.

end.text: The lesson is finished. Tap a button to go on.
